newsitem.title: UK: Guinness/Grand Met merger underlines brand value.
newsitem.headline: Guinness/Grand Met merger underlines brand value.

text.p: A trip to Burger King followed by a Haagen-Dazs ice cream or a pint of Guinness washed down by a Johnnie Walker chaser -- either way GMG Brands will serve it up.

GMG Brands, the food and drinks giant to be formed by the merger of Grand Metropolitan Plc and Guinness Plc announced on Monday, underlines the value of owning products tried and trusted by consumers around the globe.

"It's clear to us that it's brands which are driving this deal. You just have to look at what they're calling the new company," said Raymond Perrier, brand valuation director at Interbrand Group, a leading industry consultancy.
He estimated as much as 70-80 percent of the 23 billion pound-plus ($37.4 billion) worth of the new company could be down to brand strength.

Grand Met operates Burger King, Pillsbury foods, Haagen Dazs, Smirnoff vodka and Green Giant canned vegetables among other brands. Guinness, in addition to its trademark stout, has spirits such as Johnnie Walker and Bell's whisky and Gordon's gin.
GMG Brands said it will comprise four "world class" branded business units in a merger which is also expected to widen geographical cover, boost efficiences and beef up the finances.
Slogans such as "Guinness is Good for You" and reassuring advertising figures such as "The Jolly Green Giant" and "Pillsbury Dough Boy" have helped to reinforce the brands over the years.

"Both companies have phenomenally strong production but have also established very strong positions in marketing their businesses," Perrier said, adding he felt the brands were more valuable than the production side.
"It is the strength of the brand that makes customers in Malaysia or Nigeria buy Guinness rather than any other stout," he added.
"Someone else can produce the same product with the same taste or range of flavours and it won't sell as well. It's not just a case of name but design/packaging and advertising," he said.
"Branding is a pact between the producer and the consumer which must be honoured."
Perrier said the planned $20 billion telecoms merger between Britain's BT and MCI of the United States was driven in part by the desire to create a global brand to compete with AT&T Corp.
He cited British entreprenur Richard Branson's Virgin Group of companies as another prime example of brand building.
Virgin has used its youthful, iconoclastic image to market everything from bridal gowns to airline tickets.
However, brands such as Guinness, which dates back over 200 years, must be nurtured and not weakened by the pursuit of quick gains.

"My only worry is that the City will look at this and want immediate results," said Perrier, adding that price cutting and special promotions may boost short-term sales but risked robbing a product of its unique brand appeal. ($ = 0.615 British Pounds)
